prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B001 alone as my final position and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The exchange has narrowed the real questions to three, and I think each can be answered on scientific grounds. First, novelty against the 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes: the comb made optical cycles countable, and ion-trap control made single-ion clocks possible, but neither solves the problem Katori's proposal solves, which is how to interrogate thousands of neutral atoms in a lattice without Doppler, recoil or first-order light-shift errors by choosing the wavelength at which the two clock levels shift identically. That is a statement about atomic polarisabilities and level structure, which I can assess directly, and it is a different physical step. Second, independence: the 10^-18 level is reproduced at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, so the result does not depend on one laboratory. Third, attribution: Katori's concept and Ye's demonstration of record accuracy and of clock-comparison and many-body clock physics map onto two decisive contributions, and no other shortlisted configuration has a smaller gap between the credited names and the discovery. Six of eight files now prefer this exact configuration, but I do not treat that as a substitute for the argument above, and I would hold the same view if the count were lower.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses I take seriously are those I stated in round 1 and that Kroll, Mehlig and Johansson also record. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock community are outside the two names, and the three-person limit means the citation cannot cure that, only describe it honestly. The 2005 comb prize shares people and a laboratory tradition with Ye's early work, so the citation must be worded around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping, not around frequency measurement in general, to avoid reading as a second comb prize. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the impact is still prospective. I do not regard the redefinition as a precondition, because a prize recognises demonstrated performance and independent confirmation, but I accept that a colleague may weigh it differently. A further point is that I am not a neutral judge of the atomic-physics candidates, so my confidence on B001 should be discounted slightly by colleagues from other fields.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B001 with the same two names, wants the citation to cover both the invention and the 10^-18 development, treats the 2005 and 2012 overlap as presentational, and flags a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory as a possible recusal question.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your citation, and my own wording follows it closely. On your disclosure, I would not treat a past stay in Hall's laboratory as a bar, because the 2005 prize honoured Hall and Haensch for the comb and neither is credited here; what matters is that the committee records it. I would ask you to say plainly whether, as someone who knows that tradition, you think the lattice clock is a step beyond it. I think it is, and your own case_for says so, but it carries more weight coming from the person with the closest view of the comb community. I also still hold that Ye's credit is the demonstrated accuracy and clock-comparison physics and Katori's is the concept, and I see no reason why that unequal composition should block a two-name credit.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B017, argues that the open pairing mechanism does not undermine the discovery, and says he cannot judge from outside the field whether B001 is distinct from earlier clock prizes.
responses.response: You asked the atomic-physics members to say whether the lattice clock is a distinct step, so I will answer directly: it is, because the problem solved is control of the atomic environment so that a transition is insulated from the trapping field, and that is separate from counting the optical cycles or from controlling a single ion. On B017 I accept your argument that a pairing mechanism does not need to be settled for the existence of the correlated platform to be rewarded, and I have moved my position on that point. My remaining reservation is narrower than the one I stated in round 1: Cao, the first author of the decisive experiments, sits outside the three names, and the group-leader convention you propose is defensible but is a stronger choice for a field only eight years old. I would not oppose B017 in a later year and I keep it as my first alternative, but I do not think it should displace B001 now.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 as the discovery of a new regime of correlated matter, concedes that B001 has the tidier attribution, and asks whether the objection to B017 is scientific or about maturity.
responses.response: My objection is not about the quality of the science, and I will say that clearly. It is about the time horizon and the attribution gap, and in the last round you convinced me that the pairing mechanism is not itself the issue, so on that part I withdraw the point. What remains is that a new regime of matter, which you rightly value, is also being discovered in rapid sequence by many groups, and that makes the choice of three names more contestable now than it will be after a few more years of settled reproduction. I would answer your framing about clocks by saying that a 10^-18 clock is not only a refinement: it is a new regime of measurement, where gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres and many-body effects in the lattice become part of the clock physics itself. I accept that a committee wanting a discovery of a new regime of matter could prefer B017, and I would not call that unreasonable.

responses.point: Pearce proposes B001 plus B027, with Halzen alone for IceCube, but says a clocks-only prize is cleaner and that he would drop B027 if colleagues find the single-name credit unconvincing.
responses.response: I agree that B001 is the strongest single achievement and I would support it whether or not a second part is added. I do not support adding B027 this year. The chair's own case shows why: a single credited name for a collaboration-scale enterprise, source identifications at moderate significance, and thin opening support mean the second part would attract the attribution criticism that B001 avoids. You say a metrology prize and an astroparticle prize would spread the award across fields, but I do not think field balance should be a reason to add a part with weaker evidence. This is outside my specialty and I defer to you and others on the astroparticle science, but on the attribution point I take your own concession at face value and conclude that B001 alone is the right public position.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001, accepts that the comb prize is complementary, asks how the citation should weigh Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy systems, and is cautious about B002 because the credited three are experiment leaders and not the discovery analysts.
responses.response: On your citation question, I would use language that credits the concept and its realisation together, without ranking the two contributions, because the clock only exists as a joint result of the magic-wavelength idea and its demonstration at 10^-18. On B002 your attribution concern and Pearce's mention of Gianotti, Incandela and Heuer have persuaded me that I overstated how readily this configuration could be justified. I keep B002 only as a distant alternative, on the condition that the committee could defend leadership credit with a clear statement, and I would not move it above B001 or B017.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues from outside atomic physics will accept that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes, or whether the two-name credit will be criticised as insufficient for Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited; I think demonstrated independent 10^-18 performance is sufficient, but this is a judgement call.
My assessment of B017, B002 and the other non-atomic candidates relies on general knowledge, and my closeness to atomic physics may make me overrate B001.
Whether the order of Katori and Ye, and the relative weight of concept and demonstration, should appear in the citation or be left implicit.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None of Katori, Ye or the other credited names on my alternatives appears among my documented collaborators, and I have recorded no direct tie to them. I work in theoretical atomic physics, with documented collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Reinhold Schuch and others, so I disclose field proximity to B001, B032 and B042 and ask that my judgement on these be discounted accordingly. I note Kroll's Hall-laboratory disclosure and I do not think it requires recusal.
